title: Tuckpointing: Protect Yourself from Silica and Nano-Enabled Mortar Dust
summary: Grinding out mortar makes dust with respirable crystalline silica. Some mortar also contains engineered nanomaterials such as graphene. The health risk from graphene is not well understood, so keep dust out of the air and out of your lungs.
talking_points: Grinding mortar with a handheld grinder makes dust that contains respirable crystalline silica. Breathing it can cause lung cancer and scarring of the lungs.

Some mortars are nano-enabled. They have engineered nanoparticles, such as graphene, added to make them stronger. Cutting or grinding them puts those particles in the air. Animal studies suggest graphene could harm the lungs. The risk to construction workers is not well understood.

Ask your employer whether the mortar contains graphene. Check the product label and Safety Data Sheet (SDS). This information is often missing, so also check CPWR's inventory of nano-enabled products at nano.elcosh.org.
Follow OSHA's silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153) and its Table 1 for engineering controls and respirators when you grind mortar.

Use a handheld grinder with a shroud on the grinding wheel and a dust collection hose connected to a vacuum with a HEPA filter. CPWR testing found this was very effective at cutting worker exposure to graphene.

Your employer must provide the right respirator under a full respiratory protection program. N95 or P100 filters effectively capture nanomaterials. Choose one that fits the length of the mortar removal in your shift.
Wear a face shield or goggles to protect your eyes from dust, and wear hearing protection.
site_hazards_to_check: Grinders with no shroud, no vacuum hose, or a vacuum without a HEPA filter
Unknown mortar products with no SDS or no nano information on the label
Visible dust drifting from the work area toward other workers
Workers grinding without a fitted respirator, eye protection, or hearing protection
discussion_questions: How can we find out whether this mortar contains graphene or other nanomaterials?
